intro: A Melbourne songwriter who sang the way she talked, and ran her own label.
story:
Courtney Barnett was born in Sydney and made her name in Melbourne, where she put out her first songs on Milk! Records, a label she ran herself. Her voice was deadpan and wandering, and it carried her a long way from the first record. She played Pickathon in 2014, before her first full album.

That album, Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit, changed the scale of things in 2015: four ARIA Awards, the Australian Music Prize and a Grammy nomination for Best New Artist. A record with Kurt Vile followed, then Tell Me How You Really Feel.

She closed Milk! in 2023, played the farm again in 2024 and moved to Los Angeles. Creature of Habit, made there and in Joshua Tree after a long stretch of doubt, with Waxahatchee singing on one song, came out in March 2026. The critics still called it deadpan.

intro: A Chicago kid who meant to make movies, and kept a band going for nearly thirty years.
story:
Eric D. Johnson grew up in the Midwest planning to write for the movies, until a high school band changed his mind. He started Fruit Bats in 1997, put out a first album in 2001 and signed to Sub Pop the next year.

Merge signed him in 2019, and he found a second voice in Bonny Light Horseman, the folk trio he shares with Anais Mitchell and Josh Kaufman, whose first album came out in 2020.

In February 2025 he wrote and recorded Baby Man in about ten days, just his voice, guitar and piano, and he had thought of it as a stopgap. He played Pickathon that summer, fifteen years after his first visit, and Merge released the record in September. The Landfill followed in June 2026, made with a full band and named for the one kind of hill he saw growing up, the landfill beside his apartment when he was about ten.

intro: A folk troubadour who took his name from his hometown, and later made the rock record.
story:
Sean Scolnick took his stage name from his hometown, Langhorne, Pennsylvania, a place that does not sound like folk country, and made a career of it anyway. His self-titled 2008 album on Kemado set the pattern: high-energy, heart-on-sleeve folk-rock played for anyone who would listen. He came to Pickathon in 2007 and returned in 2008, 2010, 2012 and 2015.

Eleven years after that fifth visit, he made the loud record he had long wanted to make. He had met Sam Kiszka of Greta Van Fleet on tour, and the two wrote together in loose sessions at Kiszka's house. The result, The Dreamin' Kind, came out on Dualtone in January 2026 with Kiszka producing. Slim told NPR it felt like blowing up the old to plant something new, and that week he played The Daily Show with Jordan Klepper. The troubadour from a town that doesn't sound folksy had made a rock and roll album.

intro: Two North Carolina voices who started in coffee shops and later chose a new name.
story:
Andrew Marlin and Emily Frantz began playing together in 2009, in coffee shops and restaurants around Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Their first album came out in 2010 and introduced them as devoted traditionalists. By February 2019 their fifth, Tides of a Teardrop, was on Yep Roc and reached No. 2 on the Folk chart. They played Pickathon that year for the fourth time.

Then the shape of their lives changed. Their daughter, Ruby, was born in 2018, and many songs on the next album grew from that. In 2021 they dropped the name Mandolin Orange, which they had felt for a long time no longer fit, and became Watchhouse; the self-titled record came out that August on Thirty Tigers. Rituals, their eighth album and first in almost four years, followed in 2025. They still sing the same close harmonies, now under a name they chose.

intro: Four players from four corners of North America, who at their busiest played more than 300 dates a year.
story:
Caleb Klauder and Sammy Lind began Foghorn Stringband around 2000, when the founders met at the National Oldtime Fiddlers' Contest in Weiser, Idaho. The band that settled in by 2011 was four people from four places: Klauder from Orcas Island, Washington; Reeb Willms from the farmland of eastern Washington; Nadine Landry from the Gaspe coast of Quebec; and Lind from Minneapolis. At their busiest they played more than 300 dates a year.

They first came to Pickathon in 2002 and kept coming back. The 2016 set was their eighth visit. Outshine the Sun had come out in 2012 and Devil in the Seat in 2015, and a video for Columbus Stockade Blues, from that record, was shot around Portland.

Klauder and Willms later made a home in the San Juan Islands and a country record as a duo, Gold in Your Pocket, in 2024. They played the Albino Skunk festival in May 2025.

intro: A Portland bluegrass band that met in a guitar store and called its sound northwest mountain music.
story:
Jackstraw began in 1997 when Darrin Craig and Jon Neufeld met David Pugh and Jesse Withers at Artichoke Music, a Portland guitar store and acoustic music institution. They called what they played northwest mountain music, somewhere between old-time Appalachian tunes and the punk and honky-tonk sounds coming up in the Northwest.

They were on the 2001 bill and came back through 2022, seven visits in all. In April 2012 their sixth album, Sunday Never Comes, brought in banjo player Cory Goldman. Neufeld, who also plays with Black Prairie and Martha Scanlan, later produced Smithsonian Folkways' Roll Columbia: Woody Guthrie's 26 Northwest Songs, released in January 2017.

Their devoted following includes bluegrass purists, alt-country fans and kids who want to dance. They have shared bills with Del McCoury and Tim O'Brien. The 2022 set was the seventh. They still play Portland stages and the Portland FolkMusic Society's shows.

intro: A Minnesota-born singer who left for Tennessee, then a Montana ranch, and wrote songs about both places.
story:
Martha Scanlan grew up in Minnesota and moved to eastern Tennessee to be close to the music she loved, playing in the old-time string band the Reeltime Travelers. She moved to a ranch in Montana. She first played Pickathon in 2006, and her 2008 solo album, The West Was Burning, was made from that move.

She spent two years living and cowboying in a log cabin near the Wyoming border, and wrote Tongue River Stories about that place. For the next record, The Shape of Things Gone Missing, The Shape of Things to Come, she raised money on Kickstarter and went to Portland, where she recorded mostly live with members of Black Prairie and the Decemberists.

She came back to the farm in 2019 with her fourth album, The River and the Light, released in October 2018 and produced by Jon Neufeld, the Portland guitarist who tours with her as a duo.

intro: A Beaumont, Texas songwriter who started a side project and let it outgrow his old band.
story:
Kevin Russell grew up in Beaumont, Texas, and has lived within two hundred miles of the Gulf Coast his whole life. He came up through Louisiana biker bars and Austin clubs with the Gourds, and in 2007 he started Shinyribs as a solo project on the side. His first album, Well After Awhile, came out in 2010, and Gulf Coast Museum followed in 2013. The Austin Chronicle's review said the term side project no longer fit.

He played Pickathon in 2007, 2008, 2013 and 2018. The Austin Music Awards named Shinyribs Best Austin Band in 2017 and 2018, and I Got Your Medicine album of the year.

In April 2025 the Gourds played an Austin reunion show, twelve years after their last. That same month Shinyribs released Leaving Time, the ninth album, which revisits songs Russell wrote before the Gourds. Real Alligator, the tenth, followed in 2026, the first on Spaceflight Records.

intro: An Asheville band that started on a ridge above town and ended up on New West Records.
story:
Town Mountain was formed by Robert Greer and banjoist Jesse Langlais on a ridge above the Asheville skyline, with mandolinist Phil Barker joining not long after. The first Asheville stage they played was the Grey Eagle. Their first albums, Original Bluegrass and Roots Country in 2007 and Heroes and Heretics in 2008, were independent, and they toured hard enough that the International Bluegrass Music Association gave them its Momentum Award for Band of the Year.

They first played Pickathon in 2009, and came back in 2010, 2016 and 2019, by which time they had made Southern Crescent, recorded at Dirk Powell's home studio in Breaux Bridge, Louisiana, and leaned further into honky-tonk. In 2022 New West Records, the Americana label, released Lines in the Levee, their seventh album, and in November 2025 the label put out Live From Drop of Sun, a live EP.

intro: A trio that met in a Dairy Queen parking lot and lives in a log cabin in northern Michigan.
story:
Micah Middaugh and Andrea Moreno-Beals met in a Dairy Queen parking lot and started Breathe Owl Breathe in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Middaugh grew up in a small town in northern Michigan with a father who played a home-made banjo and a concertina. Moreno-Beals, born in Colombia, was a classically trained cellist. With drummer Trevor Hobbs they settled in East Jordan, in a log cabin built by Middaugh's forefathers.

They played Pickathon in 2009, 2010, 2011 and 2013. Middaugh, who is also a print-maker and draws the band's pictures, once described the sound as Leonard Cohen on an ice skating rink. In early 2009 Moreno-Beals taught grade school in Ann Arbor and Hobbs studied geology at Michigan State, so the band got together on weekends. Daytrotter recorded a session with them in January 2013, Magic Central came out that year, and Passage of Pegasus followed in October.

Audiotree counts at least seven records since 2004.

intro: A Texas banjo player who led a band that was never quite bluegrass, and moved north to find out what came next.
story:
Danny Barnes was born in Temple, Texas, and earned a degree in audio production at the University of Texas in 1985. In 1990, in Austin, he formed the Bad Livers with bassist Mark Rubin and fiddler Ralph White. He insisted they were not a bluegrass band. They played breakdowns and gospel songs, covered Motorhead and Iggy Pop, and brought in tuba, accordion and electronics.

The Bad Livers ended in 2000, and Barnes moved to Washington state, where he has worked with the jazz guitarist Bill Frisell, Dave Matthews and Chuck Leavell. He played Pickathon in 2006, 2007 and 2011. By then he was on ATO, Dave Matthews' label, which released his solo albums Pizza Box in 2010 and Rocket in 2011.

In September 2015 he won the Steve Martin Prize for Excellence in Banjo and Bluegrass, and in 2017 he made Stove Up, a tribute to the banjo player Don Stover.

intro: A Laguna Beach kid who started a punk band in high school and kept making records faster than most people hear them.
story:
Ty Segall was born in 1987 in Laguna Beach, California, and started his first punk band, Epsilons, in high school. He moved to San Francisco for university, fell in with the scene around Thee Oh Sees, and began a solo career in 2008.

He played Pickathon in 2013, 2015, 2016 and 2017. That was the year of his self-titled album, made with Steve Albini and a new live group, the Freedom Band, with Mikal Cronin, Charles Moothart, Emmett Kelly and Ben Boye, and recorded with no overdubs. The follow-up, Freedom's Goblin, ran to 19 tracks.

The Freedom Band lasted from 2016 to 2024. In 2025 he made Possession, and in 2026 he took a full band, Cronin, Kelly and Boye along with newcomer Evan Burrows, to Sonic Ranch in Texas and tracked Chrome in six days. Drag City released it on August 28.
